categories/accounting:
How to compare Accounting pricing

Accounting tools are priced per company, not per seat, and low tiers cap the things that matter: billable clients, invoices, and bank connections. FreshBooks at C$26 per month and QuickBooks Online at C$30 per month both bill in Canadian dollars; Wave is free; Xero lists its entry in the vendor's billing currency. The real comparison is the year-two price: FreshBooks' $1-per-month first year and QuickBooks' 90%-off-for-6-months intro both expire, so compute what the same plan costs after the promo before you choose, switching accounting software mid-year is painful enough that the intro rate should never decide it.

The Canadian lens matters more here than in any other category. GST/HST (and QST in Quebec) handling, CRA-compliant reporting, and clean year-end exports are worth more than a few dollars a month, and they're the reason QuickBooks' "the suite most Canadian accountants already know" tagline carries weight: an accountant who already knows your platform bills you fewer hours. If a vendor bills in USD, budget the conversion; if it bills in CAD like FreshBooks and QuickBooks, the invoice matches your books.

Reading the "From" prices above: the "From" figure is the standard list price; the badges show the current intro promos, which are separate and temporary. "From $0" at Wave is a free tier for accounting and invoicing, not a trial. All prices and promos verified 2026-09-30, and because intro offers change often, confirm the current promo terms on the vendor's site before you sign up.
categories/crm-marketing:
How to compare CRM & Marketing pricing

CRM pricing runs on two axes at once: seats and contacts. HubSpot's free tier covers unlimited users with core CRM, deals, and basic email marketing, the price stays $0 until you outgrow it. The trap is the second axis: paid hubs, marketing contacts, and sales seats are priced separately, so a "free CRM" quietly grows into a paid stack as your contact list and team grow. Map which hubs you'll actually need in year one, and price the contact tier you'll hit, not the one you start on.

Canadian buyers should read the marketing side carefully. Canada's anti-spam law (CASL) is stricter than the US CAN-SPAM rules most American tools are built around: you need consent to send commercial email, and a free tier with basic email marketing doesn't exempt you. If the vendor bills in USD, budget the conversion on top of the sticker price, and check whether the email tools support the unsubscribe and consent records CASL expects you to keep.

Reading the "From" prices above: "From $0 free" signals a free-first product with a genuinely usable free tier, verified 2026-09-30. The paid jump happens when you add a hub, add seats, or cross a contact threshold; compare on the configuration you'll be running twelve months from now, and confirm current pricing on the vendor's site before committing. If your main need is a simple contact database rather than marketing automation, the free tier may be all you ever need, many small businesses never leave it.
categories/ecommerce:
How to compare Ecommerce pricing

Ecommerce pricing has three parts and the subscription is the smallest one: the platform fee, the payment-processing cut on every sale, and add-ons (themes, apps, domains). Shopify's entry tier starts at $5 per month and Big Cartel's Gold tier is $0, but the pricing dimension is catalog size: Big Cartel gates plans by product count (5, 50, or 500 products with image limits), while Shopify gates by features and scale. Count your SKUs first, then price the tier that fits; the cheapest sticker with a catalog cap you'll outgrow in three months is the most expensive option.

Canadian sellers should check the money path, not just the monthly fee. Big Cartel bills in USD, so your card adds conversion on the paid tiers. Payment processing rates also differ by country: the rates quoted in US reviews are not necessarily what a Canadian store pays, and how you receive payouts in CAD is worth confirming before you launch. A platform that is cheap in USD can be merely average once conversion lands.

Reading the "From" prices above: "From $5 per month" is Shopify's entry tier; "From $0 free" is Big Cartel's free-forever Gold tier with a hard 5-product cap, not a trial. Neither figure includes transaction fees, which are where the real cost lives. Prices verified 2026-09-30; confirm the current plans and processing rates on each vendor's site before you build a store on them.
categories/field-service:
How to compare Field Service pricing

Field service software is priced per user per month on a plan ladder: the entry tier covers basic scheduling and invoicing, and higher tiers unlock quoting, customer management, GPS tracking, and integrations. Jobber's C$49 per month entry is billed in Canadian dollars, which takes the currency guessing out of your budget. The cost question is who needs a seat: some shops give every tech a login, others keep the software in the office and dispatch by text, the same product can cost double depending on that choice, so decide your seat policy before you price plans.

The Canadian angle is compliance and support hours. A Canadian vendor billing in CAD means the invoice total is the number you budget, no conversion surprise on the card, and support sits in your time zone, which matters when dispatch breaks at 7am and the day's routes are on the line. If you run payroll, check how the tool's exports feed whatever you use for CRA remittances and year-end; a cheap plan that can't produce a clean export costs more in bookkeeping time than it saves.

Reading the "From" prices above: "From C$49" is the entry plan's list price before add-ons, extra users above the plan's allowance, and billing-cadence discounts. Annual billing usually lowers the effective monthly rate, the Deals page shows the computed annual-billing savings per tier for the products where it applies. Prices were last confirmed 2026-09-30; confirm the current rate on the vendor's site before signing.
categories/hr-payroll:
How to compare HR & Payroll pricing

HR and payroll tools are priced per employee per month, or, as with Humi on this page, by custom quote. "Custom" means there's no published list price: you request a quote at your headcount, and the price scales with employee count plus which modules you turn on (payroll, benefits, time-off, onboarding). The only honest way to compare is at the same headcount with the same modules: a quote for 10 employees tells you nothing about the cost at 50, and a payroll-only quote tells you nothing about the full platform.

This is the category where a Canadian vendor earns its keep. Canadian payroll compliance. CRA remittances, records of employment, T4s, and provincial rules, is the whole reason to pick a Canadian-built system, and the page flags Humi as exactly that. Ask where employee data is hosted, because payroll records are the most sensitive data a small business holds. And get the quote in writing with the per-employee rate spelled out, so renewal increases don't surprise you.

Reading the prices above: "Custom" means no public list price to verify, the ✓ pill confirms the listing was checked 2026-09-30, not that a price was found. Don't treat one vendor's quote as comparable to another's until both are built on the same headcount and module list, and re-confirm before each renewal. Since there's no list price anchoring the negotiation, the per-employee rate you get quoted is the number to benchmark, get competing quotes at the same headcount and let the vendors compete.
categories/payments-pos:
How to compare Payments & POS pricing

Payments pricing is two-part: a percentage of each sale plus a fixed fee. Stripe's 2.9% + 30¢ per transaction and Square's free POS software with per-transaction pricing both follow this shape. The number that decides the winner is your average ticket: the fixed 30¢ bites harder on a $5 coffee than on a $500 invoice, so a lower percentage with a higher fixed fee favours big tickets and punishes small ones. There is no monthly fee to recover on the standard plans, the rate is the same whether you process $1,000 or $100,000, so compare on your actual ticket mix, not on volume discounts you won't get.

Canadian specifics: the 2.9% + 30¢ figure quoted here is the domestic Canadian card rate, and international cards carry extra surcharges, if you sell to US or overseas customers, price that segment separately. In-person and online rates can differ, and card readers are usually a separate hardware purchase, so check what "free POS" actually includes before you count it as zero cost. Also confirm payout timing in CAD: next-day versus two-day payouts matter to a small retailer's cash flow.

Reading the "From" prices above: Stripe's "From 2.9% + 30¢" is a rate, not a subscription, there is no base plan to upgrade from. Square's "From $0" is free software; the cost arrives per transaction. Both verified 2026-09-30; processors change rates with notice, so confirm on the vendor's pricing page before you switch.
categories/seo-marketing:
How to compare SEO & Marketing pricing

SEO tool pricing is tiered by usage limits: projects, tracked keywords, crawl credits, and seats. The entry price is only the door. Ahrefs' $29 Starter covers keyword research and competitor basics, while the full toolkit lives on higher tiers, and extra seats cost extra at both Ahrefs and Semrush. Plausible plays a different game entirely: $9 per month for up to 10,000 pageviews, priced by traffic, not seats. Compare the limits you'll actually hit (keywords tracked, sites audited, teammates with logins), because the cheapest entry tier with limits you blow through in week one is a false economy.

Canadian buyers face two gotchas in this category. First, billing is in USD at Ahrefs and Plausible, and the Semrush figures shown are the vendor's listed prices, so budget the card conversion on top of whatever currency the vendor bills in. Second, Ahrefs famously offers no free trial and no discounts: the $29 Starter tier is your evaluation cost, paid blind. That makes the entry tier's limits worth reading closely, if Starter can't answer the questions you're buying the tool for, you're really shopping the $249 Standard tier, and you should price that from the start.

Reading the "From" prices above: each figure is the lowest published monthly rate for the base tier, excluding extra seats and annual-billing discounts (annual plans save up to 17% at Ahrefs and Semrush, verify the current percentage on the vendor's site). Plausible's "From $9" is usage-based and includes a free trial, unlike the other two. All prices verified 2026-09-30.
categories/scheduling:
How to compare Scheduling pricing

Scheduling tools are priced by who gets a bookable calendar: most vendors charge per user, so the real math is the number of people who host meetings multiplied by the per-seat rate. The free tier on this page covers a single event type on one scheduling page, plenty for a solo consultant, too narrow for a sales team. When you compare plans, don't price your whole company; price the people who actually need a booking page, then check whether the tier caps (event types, calendar connections, team features) hold up at that count.

Two checks matter for Canadian buyers. First, time zones: book a test meeting across Eastern, Central, and Pacific before you roll a tool out to a team, and confirm the page handles daylight saving transitions cleanly, a mislabelled Atlantic time zone costs you no-shows. Second, look at the invoice: if the vendor bills in USD, your card adds conversion on top of the listed price, so the number you budget in CAD is higher than the sticker. Ask for a sample invoice or check the checkout currency before you commit.

Reading the "From" prices above: "From $0 free" means a genuine free tier exists, not a free trial, not a limited-time promo. Paid tiers layer on more event types, integrations, and team scheduling on top of it. Every price on this page was last confirmed 2026-09-30, and scheduling vendors quietly reshuffle tiers, so re-check the vendor's own pricing page before you buy.
categories/work-management:
How to compare Work Management pricing

Work management tools are priced per seat, and seats are the entire cost model: Monday.com's free tier covers 2 seats and basic boards, so the moment your third person needs a login, you're shopping paid plans. Per-seat pricing scales linearly, which means the honest comparison is your full team at the lowest tier that fits, not your current trial group. Also price the ceiling, not just the floor: the features that pull teams upward (automations, views, integrations, admin controls) usually live one tier above the cheapest paid plan.

For Canadian buyers, two practical checks beat any feature list. First, where your project data is hosted: ask the vendor, because data residency answers vary and your IT policy may care. Second, billing currency and support coverage, a vendor that bills in USD costs you conversion on every invoice, and support that closes before your Pacific team logs on will feel like no support at all. Neither is a dealbreaker, but both should be known before you migrate a team onto a platform.

One more cost that hides outside the per-seat price: migration effort. Moving active projects, templates, and automations off a previous tool takes real staff hours, and some vendors charge for onboarding or data import on top of the subscription. Before you commit, trial the import with a real project, not a blank board, and ask what onboarding costs in CAD. A cheaper per-seat rate paired with a paid migration can lose to a pricier seat that includes white-glove import.

Reading the "From" prices above: "From $0 free" means a real free tier, not a trial, 2 seats and basic boards here, verified 2026-09-30. Treat the free tier as the evaluation lane and the paid tiers as the actual decision; vendors in this category adjust seat caps and tier features quietly, so confirm the current limits on the vendor's pricing page before you buy.
canadian:
What the 🇨🇦 badge means

The 🇨🇦 Canadian company badge marks vendors that are Canadian businesses, the five currently tracked are FreshBooks, Shopify, Wave, Jobber, and Humi. The badge is about the vendor, not the price: a Canadian vendor usually (but not always) bills in CAD, and the price line next to each product shows the actual billing currency, with C$ marking Canadian-dollar pricing. The 🇨🇦 Canadian only checkbox in the filter bar on any listing page narrows that page down to Canadian vendors.

Why it matters: billing in CAD means no card conversion fees and invoices that match your books, support sits in your time zone, and the product is usually built around Canadian requirements. Canadian payroll compliance at Humi, GST/HST-ready invoicing at FreshBooks and Wave, Canadian home-service workflows at Jobber. None of that makes a Canadian vendor automatically the right choice, but for regulated or money-adjacent software it's a genuine head start. Every vendor and price on this page was verified 2026-09-30; confirm current pricing on the vendor's own site before buying.

How this page works

This page lists only products with a live, public promotion, right now that's FreshBooks (80% off for 4 months for new subscribers), QuickBooks Online (90% off for new subscribers), Xero (80% off your first 3 months for new customers), Shopify ($1/month for 3 months for new merchants) and Mailchimp (15% off your first 12 months, for accounts with 10,000+ contacts). A product with no current promo doesn't appear here at all; the category pages and the home page show every tracked product with its standard list price instead. Every promo on this page was confirmed on the vendor's own site on 2026-10-25, and the "Deal verification" box on each product's page records exactly what was found.

Two things to read carefully. First, the "Biggest annual-billing savings" panel below is a different kind of saving from the promos above: it's computed from verified list prices and shows what annual billing saves versus monthly at the tier level, for example, Jobber's Plus tier saves C$1,200 per year when billed annually. That saving is always available, not a limited-time offer. Second, promos expire without notice and vendors change terms quietly; the verified date tells you when the offer was last confirmed, and the vendor's own page is the final word before you buy.

Use the 🇨🇦 Canadian only filter to narrow the list to Canadian vendors, on this page that leaves FreshBooks and Shopify, which bill in CAD. Sort by price (low to high) to rank the post-promo entry prices side by side, or by name to scan the list. free:
How this page works

Every product on this page has a $0 tier, not a free trial, a tier you can stay on indefinitely. The six currently tracked: HubSpot (Free Tools, unlimited users with core CRM, deals, and basic email marketing), Monday.com (Free, up to 2 seats with basic boards), Wave (Starter, free accounting and invoicing), Square (Square POS software plus a free Appointments tier for one location), Calendly (Free, one event type on one scheduling page), and Big Cartel (Gold, 5 products with one image each). The free-notes line under each product spells out exactly what the $0 tier includes and where it caps.

The cap is the whole story with free tiers. Before you commit to one, check the limit that will hit you first: seats (Monday.com's 2-seat ceiling), products (Big Cartel's 5-product ceiling), event types (Calendly's single event type), or processing costs (Square's POS software is free, but card processing still charges per transaction, the software is free, the payments aren't). A free tier is genuinely free within its caps; the question is whether your actual usage fits inside them.

Free tiers change less often than promos, but they do change, vendors quietly adjust seat caps and feature lists. Each tier on this page was confirmed against the vendor's own pricing page on 2026-09-30, and each product's deal page shows the full pricing table so you can see what the paid upgrade costs when you outgrow $0. Confirm the current free-tier terms on the vendor's site before you build a workflow on them.
compare-index:
How to use these comparisons

Each comparison puts rival products side by side on the things that actually decide a purchase: verified list pricing taken from each vendor's own site, any current promotions running, and aggregate user feedback from G2 and Capterra. The pricing is checked and dated, each price carries its own verification date, shown on the page, see the verification log for what was checked when. Read a comparison when you're choosing between specific products, not when you're still deciding what category of software you need; the category pages and buyer's guides are the right starting point for that earlier question.

Pick the comparison that matches the decision in front of you. The accounting four-way (FreshBooks vs QuickBooks Online vs Wave vs Xero) is for choosing bookkeeping software; Square vs Stripe is for choosing how you take card payments; Semrush vs Ahrefs is for choosing an SEO toolkit. Each one names the products covered and the category up front, so you can tell at a glance whether it's the decision you're making. If the tool you're considering isn't in a comparison yet, the category page for its type still shows verified pricing for every tracked product, and the individual deal pages carry the full pricing tables.

What "verified" means

Verified means someone on the PlanPrice research team opened the vendor's own pricing page and confirmed the figures shown here, and the check date is printed next to the price. Verification dates vary by page and are printed next to the prices; the site-wide log is on the verification log. Vendors change prices and promos without notice, so a comparison is a reliable starting point, not a quote, always confirm the current price on the vendor's own site before you buy.
top-rated:
How this leaderboard is built

The "Highest average score" ranking is the mean of each product's available G2 and Capterra scores, a straight average of the two, not a PlanPrice rating. Where a product lists only one source (Shopify and Xero show G2 only; Humi shows G2 only), the average is that single score. The "Most reviewed" list is a separate signal: review count measures popularity and sample size, not quality. Both lists cover the 16 products PlanPrice currently tracks, and every score was re-checked on 2026-09-30, the date is printed in the fine print because review scores drift as new reviews land.

Read the ranking with its limits in mind. A 4.6 average built on 12 reviews (Plausible) is far thinner evidence than a 4.7 built on 23,267 (Monday.com), small review counts swing wildly with a handful of new ratings. Scores also reflect a product's whole history, not its current version, and they say nothing about price: the top of this board includes both free tiers and the priciest tools on the site. Use the leaderboard to shortlist, then check the verified pricing and the promo state on each product's deal page before you decide.

deals/ahrefs:
Canadian pricing notes

Ahrefs offers no free trial and says it never runs discounts, so the $29-per-month Starter tier is your evaluation cost, paid blind. That makes Starter's limits worth reading closely: it covers keyword research and competitor basics, while the full toolkit (site audits at scale, rank tracking, more projects) lives on the higher tiers, starting with Standard at $249 per month. Billing is in USD, so Canadian buyers pay conversion on top of every figure shown. Annual billing saves up to 17%, but confirm the current percentage on ahrefs.com before committing, and price the tier you'll actually need in six months, not just the cheapest door in.
deals/plausible:
Canadian pricing notes

Plausible's pricing is usage-based, not per-seat: the Starter tier at $9 per month covers up to 10,000 pageviews, so the "From" price on this page is the actual first paid tier rather than a teaser rate. Billing is in USD, so Canadian buyers pay the card conversion on top. There is no public promo running, the table above is standard list pricing, but a free trial is available, which is worth using to confirm your traffic fits inside the 10,000-pageview cap before you pay for the first month. If your traffic grows past the cap, the next tier up becomes the real decision, check the vendor's pricing page for the current pageview bands before you budget.
deals/stripe:
Canadian pricing notes

The 2.9% + 30¢ rate quoted here is the domestic Canadian card rate, charged per successful transaction with no setup or monthly fees. Do the per-ticket math before you compare it to anything: on a $10 sale the fixed 30¢ is the expensive half of the fee, while on a $200 invoice it's a rounding error, the same rate favours very different businesses depending on ticket size. International cards add cross-border and currency-conversion surcharges on top of the domestic rate, so price your US and overseas sales as a separate segment. Stripe doesn't run public promos, so the rate above is the rate; confirm the current terms on stripe.com before you switch processors.
deals/big-cartel:
Canadian pricing notes

Big Cartel gates its plans by catalog size, not seats: Gold is $0 forever with 5 products and one image each, Platinum is $15 per month for 50 products, and Diamond is $30 per month for 500. Billing is in USD, so Canadian sellers pay conversion on the paid tiers. The platform itself takes no cut of your sales, card processing still runs through your payment gateway at that gateway's rates, which is why the subscription looks so cheap next to a percentage-based platform. Count your SKUs before you pick: the free Gold tier is a genuine home for a five-product shop, but outgrowing it mid-season means migrating under pressure.
